items.reason: Two of the three things this item names are false at HEAD and I did not edit prose to make a text-matcher agree: sast.yml is triggered by push/pull_request/schedule and has no pull_request_target anywhere (the string exists only in explanatory comments and in the P2 rule that forbids it), and every ${{ }} in agent-review.yml already lands in an env: binding with none in a run: body — both enforced blocking by scripts/actions-pin.mjs rules P2/P5/P7 in sast.yml's `workflow-policy` job (a required check) and inside check:ci, so re-introducing either fails the build. The third question the item asks — which job genuinely needs write scope, and what would it take for the privileged half never to touch the change's code — was a real open path, and that is what I closed. The `judgment` job is the only place in the repository holding ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and `pull-requests: write` at once; it used to check out the change's tree and restore only `scripts/` and the rubric from the base, which left the rest of the change on disk next to the key — and a tree is not inert to node: the nearest package.json fixes module type and the `imports` map for every specifier the reviewer resolves, and a node_modules/ sits on the resolution path. It now records the reviewed commit as `review-head`, does `git checkout --force --detach $BASE_REF` plus `git clean -ffdx`, and passes the change as `--head` — so the change enters the privileged job only as `git diff` output, which is data. scripts/agent-review-llm.mjs gained `--head` (defaulting to HEAD, so a local run is unchanged) because the working tree is now the base and HEAD would otherwise diff against itself. How a reviewer tells it is real: `npm run test:unit` — inside `npm run check:ci`, which .husky/pre-push runs before master ships and CI runs on every push and PR — now fails with a named message if that job stops moving its tree to the base, stops cleaning, reverts to the pathspec restore, stops passing --head, or if the script stops accepting it. Not done, deliberately: no new actions-pin rule, because P2 (no pull_request_target) plus P7 (an attacker-controlled context may appear only in env:, so a checkout `ref:` cannot name one) already close the fork-to-privileged-execution class repo-wide, and a rule that can never fire is decoration. Flagged for the next scan: if this item is raised again unchanged, the detector is matching the workflows' own prose about these hazards, not the YAML.

Needs network. All 25 `uses:` references in the five workflows are first-party (actions/checkout@v7, actions/setup-node@v6, actions/upload-artifact@v7, actions/download-artifact@v7) and there are no container images, so pinning means asking api.github.com what those four tags point at right now; this session has no network and no shell, and inventing 40-hex SHAs would break every workflow rather than pin it. Answering the item's own three questions from the tree: (1) what stops actions:check from blocking is not a bug but a declared exemption — STRICT = false plus RATCHET.pinned = 0 in scripts/actions-pin.mjs make '0 of 25 pinned' a green run, and `npm run actions:pin` closes it in one pass, rewriting each ref to `action@<sha> # <tag>` AND writing STRICT = true and the ratchet floor back into the script, so the pins and their enforcement land in one reviewable diff; (2) Dependabot's github-actions ecosystem is already configured weekly in .github/dependabot.yml and reads the trailing `# <tag>` comment to offer the next bump, so the pins stay maintained rather than rotting — the maintenance cost is lower than it looks; (3) no reference is third-party, so there is no cheap partial close to take, and the exposure is the narrower 'GitHub moves its own tags' kind rather than a marketplace account. One networked command by the operator closes this: `npm run actions:pin && npm run actions:check` (must print '25 of 25'), then commit the workflows and scripts/actions-pin.mjs together. That recipe is already written verbatim in that script's header, which is the file they will open.

lessons: Check whether a scanner finding is true of the tree before treating it as work. Several D9 findings against this repository name patterns that exist only in the workflows' own comments explaining why they are forbidden — this repo documents each hazard in prose that quotes it, next to a blocking rule that refuses it. When that happens, do not soften the prose; find the question the item asks that the tree has NOT already answered (here it was the third bullet, about isolating the privileged job) and close that instead, then say plainly in the report which named observations were false so the next cycle can tell a stale detector from a real gap.

The interesting privilege boundary in an agent-authored repo is not the fork PR — GitHub already withholds secrets there. It is the same-repo branch: when nearly every branch is pushed by an agent, every branch IS handed the secrets, so a job holding a key and a write scope must not execute anything out of the change's tree. Restoring a couple of paths from the base is not enough, because `node` reads package.json for module type and the `imports` map and resolves through whatever node_modules is on disk; move the whole working tree to the base and let the change in only as `git diff` output.

This repository's unit of trust is a blocking check plus a test that fails when the wiring is removed, not a paragraph. Anything added here should end up inside `npm run check:ci` (which .husky/pre-push runs, because master ships to Vercel on push) with an assertion in test-unit/ carrying the failure message a future agent needs. Conversely, do not add a rule that cannot fire on this tree: pair the change with the existing rule that already covers the class and say so.
